text:
“Well, Father, I cannot promise you anything,” I said at last; “what you are asking of me is beyond my strength. Believe me,” I continued, seeing him make an impatient movement, “you exaggerate the consequences of this liaison. Marguerite is not the sort of girl you believe her to be. This love, far from leading me down a bad path, is capable, on the contrary, of developing the most honorable feelings in me. True love always makes one better, whoever the woman who inspires it may be. If you knew Marguerite, you would understand that I am exposing myself to no danger. She is as noble as the noblest women. As much greed as there is in others, there is just as much selflessness in her.”

“Which does not prevent her from accepting your entire fortune, for the sixty thousand francs that come to you from your mother, and that you are giving her, are—remember well what I am telling you—your only fortune.”

My father had probably saved this peroration and this threat to deal me the final blow.

I was stronger in the face of his threats than in the face of his entreaties.

“Who told you that I was going to hand that sum over to her?” I replied.

“My notary. Would an honest man have drawn up such a deed without warning me? Well, I have come to Paris to prevent you from ruining yourself for the sake of a girl. When your mother died, she left you enough to live honorably, not enough to lavish gifts upon your mistresses.”

“I swear to you, Father, Marguerite knew nothing of this gift.”

“Then why were you making it?”

“Because Marguerite, this woman whom you slander and whom you want me to abandon, is sacrificing everything she possesses in order to live with me.”

“And you accept that sacrifice? What sort of man are you, sir, to allow a Mademoiselle Marguerite to sacrifice anything for you? Come, that is enough. You will leave this woman. A moment ago I was asking you; now I order you. I will not have such filth in my family. Pack your trunks and prepare to follow me.”

“Forgive me, Father,” I then said, “but I will not leave.”

“Because?…”

“Because I have already reached the age when one no longer obeys an order.”

My father turned pale at this reply.

“Very well, sir,” he resumed; “I know what remains for me to do.”

He rang.

Joseph appeared.

“Have my trunks taken to the Hôtel de Paris,” he said to my servant. At the same time, he went into his room, where he finished dressing.

When he reappeared, I went to meet him.

“Will you promise me, Father,” I said to him, “not to do anything that might cause Marguerite pain?”

My father stopped, looked at me disdainfully, and contented himself with replying:

“You are mad, I believe.”

After which he went out, violently closing the door behind him.

I went downstairs in my turn, took a cabriolet, and left for Bougival.

Marguerite was waiting for me at the window.




Chapter XXI


“At last!” she cried, throwing her arms around my neck. “Here you are! How pale you are!”

Then I told her about my scene with my father.

“Oh, my God! I suspected as much,” she said. “When Joseph came to tell us that your father had arrived, I shuddered as though at the news of some misfortune. Poor darling! And it is I who am causing you all this sorrow. Perhaps you would do better to leave me than to fall out with your father. Yet I have done nothing to him. We live very quietly, and we are going to live more quietly still. He knows very well that you must have a mistress, and he ought to be glad that it is I, since I love you and aspire to no more than your means allow. Did you tell him how we have arranged our future?”

“Yes, and that is what irritated him most, for he saw in that decision proof of our mutual love.”

“What are we to do, then?”

“Remain together, my dear Marguerite, and let this storm pass.”

“Will it pass?”

“It will have to.”

“But your father will not leave it at that.”

“What do you expect him to do?”

“How should I know? Everything a father can do to make his son obey him. He will remind you of my past life and will perhaps do me the honor of inventing a few new stories to make you abandon me.”

“You know very well that I love you.”

“Yes, but what I also know is that sooner or later one must obey one’s father, and perhaps you will end by allowing yourself to be persuaded.”

“No, Marguerite, it is I who will persuade him. It is the gossip of some of his friends that is causing this great anger; but he is good, he is just, and he will reconsider his first impression. Besides, after all, what do I care!”

“Do not say that, Armand; I would rather endure anything than let it be thought that I am setting you against your family. Let today pass, and tomorrow return to Paris. Your father will have reflected on his side, as you have on yours, and perhaps you will understand one another better. Do not clash with his principles; appear to make a few concessions to his wishes; seem not to care quite so much for me, and he will leave things as they are. Hope, my darling, and be quite certain of one thing: whatever happens, your Marguerite will remain yours.”

“Do you swear it to me?”

“Do I need to swear it to you?”

How sweet it is to let oneself be persuaded by a voice one loves! Marguerite and I spent the whole day repeating our plans to each other, as though we had understood the need to carry them out more quickly. At every moment we expected some event, but fortunately the day passed without bringing anything new.

The next day, I left at ten o’clock and reached the hotel around noon.

My father had already gone out.

I went to my rooms, where I hoped he might perhaps have gone. No one had come. I went to my notary’s. No one!

I returned to the hotel and waited until six o’clock. Monsieur Duval did not return.

I set off again for Bougival.

I found Marguerite no longer waiting for me as on the previous day, but seated by the fire, which the season already made necessary.

She was sufficiently absorbed in her thoughts to let me approach her armchair without hearing me and without turning around. When I placed my lips on her forehead, she started as though that kiss had awakened her with a jolt.

“You frightened me,” she said to me. “And your father?”

“I did not see him. I do not know what this means. I found him neither at his hotel nor in any of the places where there was a possibility that he might be.”

“Well, it will have to be done again tomorrow.”

“I am strongly inclined to wait until he sends for me. I believe I have done everything I ought to do.”

“No, my darling, that is not enough; you must go back to your father, especially tomorrow.”
